extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science, biology, and philosophy of science; readers evaluating scientific hypotheses about life and evolution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for constructing and assessing scientific hypotheses (especially about life and its origin), emphasizing conceptual models that classify perceptual experience, their empirical scope, and distinctions between physical and biological forms of selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define life by secondary characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between the inorganic and the organic cannot be defined by saying that the one is mechanical and the other is not. We are ultimately obliged, in order to define life, to take secondary characteristics — to describe the structure by which we conceptualize the organic corpuscle, the motions which are peculiar to it, and the environment in which alone we perceive life to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify atomic/chemical structure (complex compounds of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen; protein/protoplasm with water), characteristic movements (inner growth rather than surface accretion; cyclical changes including reproduction/division), and environmental requirements (certain moisture and temperature conditions). These characteristics together suffice to mark off the organic from the inorganic; definitions should enumerate such secondary traits rather than rely on vague metaphysical distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not define life by asserting mechanism cannot explain it
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who say mechanism cannot describe life are going far beyond what is justifiable in the present state of our knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid invoking an unexplained metaphysical gap between mechanism and life; instead employ describable secondary characteristics and remain cautious about claiming current mechanistic explanations are final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring spontaneous generation from observed reversibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiom omne vivum e vivo is closely associated with many important problems... The argument [for spontaneous generation] would only be valid if we could assert that all sequences of sense-impressions are reversible, but this is too wide a statement to be laid down unrestrictedly in the present state of scientific knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conclude life arose from lifeless substance simply because living things can become lifeless; require independent evidence for reversibility of the relevant sequences (consider irreversibility such as energy degradation). Laboratory failure to reproduce spontaneous generation is not decisive if the process may have taken geological timescales and irreversible steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific hypotheses must be conceptual models that classify perceptual experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of science is to classify and resume in brief formulae the phases of our perceptual experience. It has to knit together all our sense-impressions by conceptual links, and thus to enable us to take a wide survey of the universe with the least possible expenditure of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good scientific hypothesis should (a) summarize observed phenomena, (b) link perceptions across time (past and future) by flowing from laws that accurately describe present perceptual experience, and (c) economize thought. Treat hypotheses as descriptive shorthand rather than metaphysical substrata; their scientific validity depends on agreement with observations where comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject hypotheses invoking 'ultra-scientific' or metaphysical causes as science
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis of a 'special creation' cannot be accepted as part of a conceptual model of the universe; it cannot serve — like the formula of evolution — as a means of linking together phases of our perceptual experience: it would not bring unity into the phenomena of life nor enable us to economize thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept untestable, metaphysical explanations (an 'ultra-scientific cause') as scientific contributions. Prefer hypotheses that can be incorporated into conceptual models linking and predicting perceptual data; invoking the supernatural simply cloaks ignorance and is incompatible with the scientific aim of striving to know.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrapolate models only where model and observations agree
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity of the conceptual curve for representing the phenomenal curve within the sphere of our perceptions would not be invalidated if the phenomenal curve came to a full stop beyond the sphere of perception... The sole basis of our assertion that the model can be used to describe the non-perceptible past and future is that the conceptual model and our perceptual experience agree at all points where we can compare them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use agreement between model and observed data in the examined domain as the criterion for justified extrapolation into unobserved past/future; quantify/measure the extent of agreement when possible (analogy: two curves touching over a known arc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish physical selection from natural selection when assessing evolutionary explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two elements in natural selection — environment, which may be either organic or inorganic, and death, as a process of eliminating those less fitted to this environment... In the case of purely inorganic substances ... a physical selection of stable and destruction of unstable products might go on. This physical selection is not precisely the same as natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying Darwinian-style selection, determine whether the environment is inorganic (favoring stability of compounds; 'physical selection' by dissolution or stability) or organic (competition among organisms; biological/natural selection where 'death' eliminates unfit organisms). For origin-of-life stages very close to inorganic chemistry, physical selection may dominate; biologists must specify when natural selection becomes the governing factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate origin-of-life hypotheses on empirical plausibility and explanatory economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Three hypotheses: (a) perpetuity of life (immortal organic corpuscle), (b) spontaneous generation (abiogenesis), (c) special creation. The perpetuity hypothesis requires extensive inferences about primordial life capable of withstanding unlike environments and is less adequate than others; spontaneous generation postulates chemical evolution culminating in protoplasm and, despite laboratory failures, may be satisfactory; special creation fails to function as scientific explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess origins hypotheses by (a) how well they allow linking and classifying perceptual experience without gratuitous metaphysical assumptions, (b) their need for additional physical information (e.g., conditions in the azoic period), and (c) whether they economize thought and permit conceptual continuity. Laboratory reproducibility is desirable but absence of short-term experimental demonstration is not decisive if the process plausibly required geological timescales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat conceptual symbols as descriptive shorthand, not explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is the description in conceptual shorthand of the various phases of our perceptual experience, and the very statement of the hypothesis — as 'the operation in time of some ultra-scientific cause' — shows that we have gone beyond knowledge... the mystery lies at hand in every change of sense-impression, in the fact that knowledge is at all times a description, but never an explanation of that change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reifying theoretical constructs (forces, molecular structures, selection) into ultimate explanations; recognize models as tools for summarizing perception. This cautions against claiming that physics/chemistry 'explain' phenomena beyond providing descriptive shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret historical/social phenomena through natural-history scientific formulae to make history scientific
rubrics_metrics.description: History can never become science ... until these facts are seen to fall into sequences which can be briefly resumed in scientific formulae. The growth of national and social life can give us the most wonderful insight into natural selection, and the elimination of the unstable on the widest and most impressive scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For historical or social analysis to be scientific, seek patterns and sequences that permit concise scientific generalizations (e.g., analogues of natural selection). Encourage interdisciplinary application of biological descriptive frameworks where appropriate, but beware of inappropriate literalism.
